drills.name: Streamline position
drills.desc: Hands stacked, arms squeezed behind the ears, body long and rigid off every push-off. Streamline is the fastest you will ever move in the water, so every meter of glide is free speed. The position is held by the lats and core, not by the hands alone.
mistakes: Arms wide of the head instead of squeezed behind the ears.
Arching the lower back, which drags the hips and legs down.
Breaking streamline early instead of gliding to race speed before kicking.

drills.name: Side-kick and rotation drill
drills.alt: Kicking on your side to learn body roll
drills.desc: Kicking on one side with the bottom arm extended, then rotating to the other side every six kicks. Freestyle power comes from the body rolling as one unit around its long axis — this drill teaches the hips and shoulders to rotate together while the head stays still.
mistakes: Rotating the shoulders while the hips stay flat — they must roll together.
Lifting the head to breathe instead of rolling with the body.
Bending at the waist so the body snakes instead of rotating on one axis.

drills.name: Bilateral breathing
drills.alt: Breathing to both sides every three strokes
drills.desc: Breathing on alternate sides every three strokes, exhaling steadily underwater so the inhale is a quick sip in the bow-wave trough. Balances the stroke, evens out body roll, and removes the panic-breath — the exhale underwater is the real skill.
mistakes: Holding the breath underwater then trying to exhale and inhale in one turn.
Lifting the head forward to breathe, which sinks the hips.
Over-rotating to the sky on the breathing side.

drills.name: Breathing pattern sets
drills.desc: Repeats swum on fixed patterns — breathe every 3, 5, then 7 strokes by 25s — teaching CO2 tolerance and a calm, full exhale. Racing demands fewer breaths off turns and into finishes; this builds that comfort without breath-holding heroics. Never done to failure and never alone.
mistakes: Holding air in instead of trickling a steady exhale between breaths.
Letting stroke technique collapse just to hit the pattern.
Turning it into hypoxic max-breath-hold games — that's dangerous, not training.

drills.name: Catch-up drill
drills.alt: One arm waits for the other
drills.desc: Full freestyle where each hand waits extended out front until the other completes its stroke and touches it. Exaggerates front-quadrant timing and a long bodyline, forcing patience in the glide and one clean stroke at a time.
mistakes: Pausing dead in the water instead of keeping a light kick going.
Letting the waiting hand sink below the surface.
Rushing the touch and losing the drill's whole point — patience out front.

drills.name: Fingertip drag drill
drills.desc: Freestyle with the fingertips dragging along the surface during each recovery, forcing the elbow to lead high and the arm to stay relaxed. A high, loose recovery keeps the stroke compact and protects the shoulder over thousands of repetitions.
mistakes: Swinging a straight arm wide over the water instead of leading with the elbow.
Gripping tension in the hand — the fingertips should barely tickle the surface.
Letting body rotation die because attention is on the arm.

drills.name: Freestyle catch (early vertical forearm)
drills.alt: Getting the forearm vertical early to grip the water
drills.desc: Tipping the fingertips down and popping the elbow high right after entry, so forearm and hand form one big paddle pressing water backward. This early vertical forearm is the single biggest propulsion upgrade in freestyle — the pull comes from the lats, with the elbow staying above the hand until the finish.
mistakes: Dropping the elbow and pulling through with a straight arm — pushes water down, not back.
Crossing the midline at entry, which snakes the bodyline.
Starting the pull before the fingertips have tipped down and caught.

drills.name: Flutter kick sets
drills.desc: Repeated lengths with a kickboard or in streamline, kicking from the hips with long, loose ankles and a narrow amplitude. The kick's job in distance freestyle is balance and body position more than thrust — it comes from the hip, with the knee soft and the ankle floppy.
mistakes: Kicking from the knees like riding a bicycle instead of from the hips.
Stiff, dorsiflexed ankles that push water forward and brake the body.
A huge splashy amplitude — the kick should stay inside the body's shadow.

drills.name: Pull sets with buoy and paddles
drills.desc: Freestyle with a pull buoy between the thighs, often with paddles, isolating the upper body. The buoy lifts the hips so all attention goes to catch, pull path, and connecting each stroke to core rotation. Paddles add load — earn them with clean technique first.
mistakes: Using paddles so big the elbow drops and the shoulder takes the strain.
Letting the legs snake behind the buoy instead of holding a quiet core.
Pulling wide of the bodyline instead of pressing water straight back.

drills.name: Underwater dolphin kick
drills.desc: Streamlined dolphin kicks off each wall, driving the wave from the chest through the hips to the toes in both directions — down-kick and up-kick. Called the fifth stroke because elite racers carry wall speed further underwater than anyone can swim on the surface.
mistakes: Kicking only from the knees with a rigid torso — the wave must start at the chest.
A strong down-kick but a dead up-kick; both directions propel.
Staying under past 15 meters or beyond what breath control safely allows.

drills.name: Backstroke basics
drills.alt: Body position and rhythm on your back
drills.desc: Flat head, hips high, and a steady flutter kick while the arms alternate — pinky-first entry, deep catch, and a strong push past the hip. Like freestyle, the power comes from shoulder-and-hip roll around a still head; the face stays dry and the body stays long.
mistakes: Sitting in the water with dropped hips instead of lying flat.
Lifting the head to look at the feet, which sinks everything.
Thumb-first hand entry that torques the shoulder.

drills.name: Breaststroke pull-breathe-kick-glide
drills.desc: The stroke lives or dies on sequence: insweep and breathe, then drive the whip kick as the arms shoot forward, then hold a full glide. Propulsion comes from the kick snapping the feet back and together while the body is at its longest — kick into the glide, never into the pull.
mistakes: Pulling and kicking at the same time so they cancel each other out.
A screw kick with one foot turned in — asymmetry that strains the knee.
Skipping the glide and rushing into the next stroke.

drills.name: Butterfly basics
drills.desc: Both arms recover over the water while the body undulates through two dolphin kicks per cycle — one as the hands enter, one as they exit. Fly is rhythm, not muscle: press the chest down, let the hips rise, and let the kick finish what the bodyline starts. Fighting the water flat is what makes it exhausting.
mistakes: Muscling the arms over a flat body instead of letting undulation lead.
Lifting the whole chest skyward to breathe rather than sliding the chin forward.
Missing the second kick, which leaves the hips sinking at the finish of the pull.

drills.name: Open turns
drills.alt: Two-hand touch turns for fly and breast
drills.desc: A two-hand wall touch, then knees drive to the chest as one arm slices back and the body spins to plant the feet. The turn is won by a compact tuck and an explosive leg drive into a deep streamline — touch, spin, plant, push.
mistakes: Gliding into the wall and touching with bent, dead arms.
Spinning flat on the surface instead of tucking small and low.
Pushing off on the surface instead of leaving the wall in streamline underwater.

drills.name: Flip turns
drills.alt: Freestyle tumble turn at the wall
drills.desc: A forward somersault initiated one stroke from the wall, feet planted shoulder-width, then an explosive push-off on the back twisting into streamline. Speed comes from carrying momentum into the tumble — chin tucks, hips snap over, and the wall is hit with bent legs loaded to fire.
mistakes: Gliding into the wall and flipping from a dead stop.
Flipping too far away and pushing off with straight legs — no power.
Lifting the head to sight the wall on the last stroke instead of using the T on the bottom.

drills.name: Open-water sighting
drills.desc: Lifting just the eyes above the surface at the top of a stroke — crocodile eyes — then rolling into a normal side breath. Sighting is timed with a stronger kick beat so the hips stay high; lift small, look fast, and swim straight between looks. Crooked swimming costs more time than slow swimming.
mistakes: Lifting the whole head and shoulders, which drops the hips like an anchor.
Sighting and breathing in the same forward lift instead of separating them.
Sighting every two strokes out of anxiety — trust the line, look every 6-10.
